newsitem.title: USA: Boeing, Lockheed, TRW get $1.1 bln USAF deal.
newsitem.headline: Boeing, Lockheed, TRW get $1.1 bln USAF deal.

text.p: Boeing Co said on Tuesday a team of Boeing, TRW Inc and Lockheed Martin was awarded a $1.1 billion contract from the U.S. Air Force to develop and flight test a laser weapon system.
The project will develop a U.S. military airborne laser to destroy tactical ballistic missiles in flight, the Air Force added in a separate statement.
The Boeing-led will develop a prototype laser to be mounted on a Boeing 747 aircraft in the next six years to see if it can burn up short and medium-range missiles shortly after they are launched.
The Boeing team defeated a team headed by Rockwell International Corp. That team included General Motors Corp's Hughes aircraft division and the E-Systems unit of Raytheon Corp.

Under the so-called Program Definition and Risk Reduction contract, the companies, working together as Team ABL, would build and test an Airborne Laser weapon system mounted aboard a Boeing 747-400F freighter aircraft, Boeing said.
The laser weapon system would be designed to defend against the threat of theater ballistic missiles such as the Iraqi Scuds used during Gulf War, Boeing said.

Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Ronald Fogelman announced the award at a Pentagon press conference. He called the technology for the chemical laser "cutting edge" and said it could change the way the military thinks about defense.

While the initial work would be worth $1.1 billion, it could eventually mean tens of billions for the winning team if the space age weapon can protect troops and bases against missiles carrying nuclear, biological, chemical or conventional warheads.
The proceeds from the contract would be divided equally between the three companies on its team, Boeing said.

If the initial five-year contract was successful, the Air Force would proceed with an engineering and manufacturing development contract for a fully operational system, Boeing said. The team's prototypes would then be used as residual operational capacity, it said.
The Airborne Laser was able to cross oceans without refuelling and arrive on station within hours, Boeing said.
It would also significantly enhance the performance of other theater ballistic missile defenses through real-time transmission of precise trajectory data on multiple launches, the company said.
The U.S. Air Force envisioned having a fleet of up to seven Airborne Laser weapons, which would play a key role in U.S. defense, Boeing said.

The Airborne Laser Weapon System Program is managed by the U.S. Air Force at Kirtland Air Force Base, New Mexico. In 1994, the same Boeing, Lockheed and TRW team was one of two teams chosen by the Air Force to conduct separate Airborne Laser conceptual design studies, Boeing said.
